claims.text: Classical molecular dynamics simulations can capture the size-dependent thermal stability and structural changes of FeCuCrCoNi high-entropy alloy nanoparticles.
Smaller FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticles begin morphological transformations at lower temperatures than larger nanoparticles.
The initial FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticles are solid solutions.
The nanoparticle sizes range from a few nanometers to tens of nanometers.
A simulated temperature ramp using a many-body EAM or MEAM interatomic potential can be used to study the nanoparticles.
The proposed simulation heats the nanoparticles from room temperature to approximately 1200 K.
Systematically varying nanoparticle size isolates size effects on thermal response.
Increasing temperature drives atomic rearrangement and diffusion in FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticles.
Enhanced atomic mobility triggers composition fluctuations and morphological changes.
The structural response is size-dependent because nanoparticle size changes the surface-to-volume ratio and associated surface-energy contribution.
Smaller nanoparticles undergo structural and phase transformations at lower temperatures than larger nanoparticles.
Smaller nanoparticles develop more pronounced core-shell or phase-separated structures because of their higher surface-to-volume ratios.
At low temperatures, the nanoparticles remain stable solid solutions with minimal segregation or structural change.
Low-temperature behavior is largely independent of nanoparticle size.
Nanoparticles above approximately 10 nm or simulations at very long timescales may exhibit more complex phenomena.
The accuracy of the predicted thermal response depends on limitations of the selected interatomic force field.
